name: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
info: Nzinga Mbande (c. 1583 – 1663), called Ngola Njinga by her people, was queen of the Ambundu kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day Angola, remembered for decades of war and diplomacy against Portuguese expansion.

facts.born: c. 1583 in the royal family of Ndongo; daughter of Ngola Kilombo and Kengela ka Nkombe, one of his slave wives
facts.died: 17 December 1663 in Matamba, in her sleep, after an infection of the throat spread to her lungs
facts.role: Ambassador of Ndongo to the Portuguese in Luanda, 1621–1622; ruler (Ngola) of Ndongo from 1624; queen of Matamba from 1631
facts.known: The embassy to Luanda and her baptism as Ana de Sousa; war against the Portuguese from 1626; the conquest of Matamba; the alliance with the Dutch West India Company; the peace treaty of 1656; her place as a symbol of Angolan resistance

t: Nzinga took power in Ndongo in 1624 and fought Portuguese expansion for some thirty years, first in exile, then from the kingdom of Matamba, which she conquered between 1631 and 1635.

She was a diplomat as much as a soldier: she negotiated with the Portuguese, allied with the Imbangala and the Dutch, and in 1656 made a peace that recognised her rule and gave her a monopoly of the slave trade.
Her wars were financed by the slave trade she expanded, and historians such as Linda Heywood caution against portraying her as either a populist hero or a tyrant.
dyk: Her name is said to come from a difficult birth: the umbilical cord was wrapped around her neck, and the Kimbundu verb kujinga means to twist or turn.
ev: Nzinga leads Ndongo's embassy to the Portuguese governor in Luanda and is baptized as Ana de Sousa
After her brother Ngola Mbandi dies, Nzinga takes power in Ndongo and the title of Ngola
The Portuguese declare war on Nzinga and recognise her rival Hari a Kiluanje as king
Nzinga captures and deposes Queen Mwongo Matamba and takes the throne of Matamba
Nzinga allies with the Dutch West India Company after the Dutch seize Luanda
With Dutch reinforcements Nzinga defeats the Portuguese at the Battle of Kombi and besieges Massangano
Nzinga signs a peace treaty with Portugal, making the Lucala River the border
Nzinga dies in Matamba and her sister Kambu succeeds her

sections.early:
Nzinga Mbande was born around 1583 into the royal family of Ndongo, a Mbundu kingdom in what is now northern Angola. She was the daughter of Ngola Kilombo, who became king in 1593, and of Kengela ka Nkombe, one of his slave wives and his favourite concubine. Legend says her birth was difficult and that she was named for the umbilical cord wrapped around her neck; royal children who survived such births were believed to have spiritual gifts. She had two sisters, Kambu and Funji, and a brother, Mbandi, the heir.

Because she was not an heir, her father could favour her without offending his likelier successors. She was trained as a warrior with the battle axe, the traditional weapon of Ndongo, took part in legal and war councils and important rituals, and learned to read and write Portuguese from visiting missionaries. Ndongo was then in crisis. The Portuguese had set up a trading post at Luanda in 1575, and decades of war followed in which they burned villages, took hostages, built forts and seized large numbers of slaves (50,000 according to one source). In 1607 the Imbangala, bands of warriors, invaded the kingdom as well.
sections.rise:
When her father died in 1617, her brother Ngola Mbandi took the throne and killed many rivals. Nzinga was spared, but he had her young son killed and had her and her sisters forcibly sterilized; she fled to Matamba. In 1621 he asked her to be his envoy to the Portuguese in Luanda, as she was royal and spoke fluent Portuguese. A popular story tells that she was offered only a mat to sit on before the governor, João Correia de Sousa, and that an attendant made herself a seat for her. She offered peace, the return of escaped slaves and entry for Portuguese traders, but demanded the removal of the forts and refused tribute, saying only conquered peoples paid it. She was baptized in Luanda as Dona Ana de Sousa, and a treaty was agreed.

The peace did not hold. The Portuguese kept their forts and raided Ndongo for loot and slaves, and her brother fell into deep depression. When he died in 1624, of mysterious causes, Nzinga had her supporters seize the royal ritual objects, removed her opponents and took the title of Ngola. She married the Imbangala chief Kaza, guardian of her seven-year-old nephew, and then had the boy killed, in her view revenge for her own son. Rival nobles held that a woman, and a child of a slave wife, could not rule.
sections.deeds:
Nzinga sent messengers to urge slaves to flee Portuguese plantations, and many sobas, the nobles, joined her. The Portuguese backed the rebel soba Hari a Kiluanje and declared war on her on 15 March 1626. Defeated, she lost half her army and her two sisters in an ambush and by late 1628 had perhaps 200 soldiers left. She then allied with the Imbangala warlord Kasanje, married him and was initiated into Imbangala society; historian Linda Heywood describes her combining her Mbundu heritage with Imbangala military tradition to form a new army. Between 1631 and 1635 she conquered the Kingdom of Matamba, which had a tradition of female rule, and made it her base. There she took male titles and dress.

She expanded the slave trade, selling to the Dutch as many as 13,000 slaves a year. When the Dutch West India Company seized Luanda in 1641 she allied with them, built a war camp of 80,000 people and reclaimed large parts of Ndongo between 1641 and 1644. She defeated the Portuguese at Ngoleme in 1644 and, with Dutch help, at Kombi in 1647, and besieged Massangano, but lacking artillery she could not take it. In 1648 the Portuguese retook Luanda and the Dutch left Angola.
sections.opponents:
Nzinga's enemies were the Portuguese colonial government, the nobles who backed their candidates Hari a Kiluanje and then Ngola Hari, and at times Kasanje and Garcia II of Kongo, whose Wandu region she seized. The Portuguese rejected her offer of vassalage in 1627 and beheaded her envoy; after her defeat at Kavanga in 1646 her sister Funji, found to have spied for her, was reputedly drowned by them in the Kwanza River. Her rule was also harsh on her own side: her soldiers in Matamba killed and ate many people, as Heywood notes, and she told European visitors that she tolerated the custom among her soldiers but did not share it.

She built her power on the slave trade and, after her return to Christianity, had the shrines of traditionalist priests burned and some of the priests sold as slaves to the Portuguese. Her reputation was shaped by hostile writers. The Capuchin Antonio Cavazzi called her a queen who had ruined the land, and his account includes charges, such as cannibalism, for which he offers no evidence; legends of her killing her lovers have no proof. Joseph C. Miller criticised her autocratic methods, and Aurora Levins Morales her part in the slave trade.
sections.last:
After 1648 Nzinga worked to keep the Portuguese from pushing inland rather than to reconquer Ndongo. From 1644 she had admitted captured missionaries to her court; the Spanish Capuchin Calisto Zelotes do Reis Mago became her secretary, and she sought support through them from the Vatican, receiving a letter from Pope Alexander VII in 1661. Peace talks began in 1651 and ended in a treaty in late 1656: she ceded her western coast, the Lucala River became the border, the slave trade was concentrated in a market at her capital, and her sister Kambu was released, reaching her court on 12 October.

In her last years she rebuilt Matamba as a trading power, resettled former slaves, allowed women in her camp to bear children, reformed the law, abolished concubinage and married her favourite concubine in a Christian ceremony. Fearing a succession crisis after a serious illness in 1657, she named Kambu her heir. In October 1663 she fell ill with an infection of the throat, which spread to her lungs, and she died in her sleep on 17 December 1663. She was buried with Catholic and Mbundu rites, and Kambu, known as Dona Barbara, took the throne.
sections.legacy:
Oral traditions celebrating Nzinga began immediately after her death and persisted after her kingdoms were absorbed into Portuguese Angola. In the 20th century she became a symbol of Angolan resistance in the war of independence and was embraced by the People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola. She is remembered as the Mother of Angola; a major street in Luanda bears her name, a statue of her was placed at Kinaxixi in 2002, and the National Reserve Bank of Angola issued a 20 kwanza coin in her honour in 2014. In the 104 years after her death, queens ruled her kingdom for at least eighty.

Her image changed with her writers. The Capuchins Antonio da Gaeta (1669) and Cavazzi (1689) wrote the main early biographies; Jean-Baptiste Labat's 1732 version of Cavazzi led 18th- and 19th-century Western writers, among them the Marquis de Sade, to dwell on her alleged cruelty and cannibalism. From the 20th century historians took a more nuanced view: John Thornton stressed her struggle for authority and her place in Atlantic Creole culture, and Linda Heywood, in her 2017 biography, describes a complicated ruler who used culture, diplomacy, religion and war to secure her kingdom.

summary: Nzinga Mbande ruled Ndongo from 1624 and Matamba from 1631, fighting Portuguese expansion for some thirty years through war, exile and alliances with the Imbangala and the Dutch, before a peace in 1656. Her wars rested on the slave trade she expanded; she died in 1663 and is remembered in Angola as the Mother of Angola.
references: Onwuka N. Njoku, Mbundu (The Rosen Publishing Group, Inc., 1997)
Willie F. Page, Encyclopedia of African History and Culture: From Conquest to Colonization (1500-1850) (Facts on File, 2001)
Sylvia Serbin, African Women, Pan-Africanism and African Renaissance (UNESCO, 2015)
notes: The article names her Imbangala husband 'Kaza' in one section and 'Kasanje' in the next; they may be the same man or not. I named Kaza for the nephew episode and Kasanje for the alliance, as each section does.

The article dates the treaty of her embassy both 1621 (in a later section) and late 1622 (when she returned); her conversion is also dated 1623 in the Christianity section, against her baptism during the 1621-1622 embassy. I used 1621 for the embassy and avoided a conversion year.
The article's 1624 assassination/succession: brother died 'of mysterious causes (some say suicide, others say poisoning)'; kept as 'mysterious causes'.
Left out: the Imbangala initiation details (blood oath, infant oil), as the article says sources disagree; the Dapper harem legend beyond 'legends ... have no proof'.
Her father's death year 1617 is given as Ngola Mbandi Kiluanji's in the article.
